paras.text: Michigan Licensing Law and Exam Logistics, Audio Lecture

Before we start, let me tell you why this chapter is worth more than any other hour you will spend. On the business and law half of your exam there are fifty questions, and thirteen of them come out of this chapter alone. That is better than one in four.

And here is the good part. Code questions make you apply a rule to a situation. These questions just ask whether you know the law. No judgment, no interpretation. That makes this the most reliable block of points on the whole exam.

So I am not going to read you a list of rules. I am going to teach you eight ideas, one at a time, and after each one I will ask you a question and then be quiet while you answer it out loud. Answer out loud. The answer you can say is the answer you own.
Idea one. Who is in charge here, and under what law.

Michigan licenses residential builders under Article twenty four of the Occupational Code. That is Public Act two ninety nine of nineteen eighty, and the sections run from M C L three thirty nine point two four zero one through two four one two. Hold onto that range. Almost everything in this chapter lives inside those twelve sections.

The agency that runs the program is LARA, the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, through its Bureau of Construction Codes. Sitting alongside LARA is a board, and the exam likes its makeup. It is the Residential Builders and Maintenance and Alteration Contractors Board. Nine members. Four licensed residential builders, two licensed M and A contractors, and three members of the public.
Nine, four, two, three. Notice the trades outnumber the public, but not by much. If a question offers you a board where the public members outnumber the builders, that is wrong.

Two framework facts that catch people out. Michigan does not license commercial builders at the state level. Article twenty four is residential only. And Michigan has no reciprocity with any other state. A builder licensed in Ohio for thirty years starts here from zero.
Question for you. Under what act and what section range does Michigan license residential builders, and how many people sit on the board. Say it out loud.

Article twenty four of the Occupational Code, Public Act two ninety nine of nineteen eighty, sections two four zero one through two four one two. Nine board members, four builders, two M and A, three public. If that came out slowly, that is fine. It is the first time.
Idea two. What counts as a residential structure.
This one matters because the whole licensing scheme only applies to residential structures. If the building is not one, Article twenty four does not touch it.

Under the current statute a residential structure is one of two things. A detached one or two family dwelling. Or a townhouse of not more than three stories above grade plane with a separate means of egress.
Say that back. Detached one or two family. Or a townhouse, three stories or less, separate egress.

Now here is the trap, and it is a good one because it used to be true. This definition was rewritten in twenty twenty. Older study books talk about combination residential and commercial structures, and about counting units. If an answer choice tells you that any building of three units or less is a residential structure, that is the trap. Unit count alone is not the test. The test is the two shapes I just gave you.
Question. A four story townhouse with a separate entrance for each unit. Residential structure under Article twenty four, yes or no.
No. Three stories above grade plane is the ceiling. Four stories falls out of the definition, separate egress or not.
Idea three. Who is a builder, who is an M and A contractor, and why a flipper gets caught.

A residential builder is anyone who, for compensation other than wages for personal labor only, undertakes or offers to undertake construction, repair, alteration, improvement, wrecking, or demolition of a residential structure.

Read that sentence again in your head and find the word offers. It is doing enormous work. Offering to undertake the job counts. You can violate the licensing law standing in a homeowner's kitchen, before you have driven a single nail, if you offer to do work you are not licensed to do.

The definition also sweeps in anyone dealing in prefabricated, precut, packaged, or shell housing, and anyone who erects a residential structure, except on their own property for their own use and occupancy.
Now the maintenance and alteration license, the M and A. It covers repair, alteration, additions, improvement, wrecking, building a garage, and laying concrete on residential property.

Here is the relationship you need, because they will test it. A residential builder license covers everything an M and A license covers. But an M and A contractor cannot do new construction. Builder is the bigger license. Think of it as one circle inside another, with new construction sitting in the outer ring only.

And the M and A definition catches house flippers. If you buy, substantially rehab, and resell the same residential structure more than twice in one calendar year, you need a license. Two exits. If it is for your own use and occupancy, or if you hire all the work out to licensed contractors, you are clear.
Question. You rehab and sell three houses this calendar year, doing the work yourself. Licensed or not licensed.
You need the license. More than twice in one calendar year is the line, and three is more than twice. If you had subbed every bit of the work to licensed contractors, you would be outside it.

One more definition while we are here, and it is small. A salesperson is an employee or agent, other than a qualifying officer, of a licensed builder or contractor, who sells or solicits contracts for the licensee's services. Occasional and incidental sales do not count.
Idea four. When you need no license at all.

The exemptions live in section two four zero three. Government representatives. An owner building on their own property for their own use and occupancy. An owner of rental property doing maintenance and alteration on that rental property. Officers of a court. Subcontractors working solely under contract with a licensed builder. And licensed electrical, plumbing, and mechanical contractors, but only for their own trade work.
Then there is the famous one. If the aggregate price for labor, materials, and everything else on one undertaking is less than six hundred dollars, no license is required.
Now watch, because two things hang off that number and the exam tests both.

The first is the anti evasion clause. You cannot slice a large job into a stack of little contracts under six hundred dollars to dodge the act. If the work is part of a larger operation, the exemption is gone. Picture a full bathroom remodel written up as four separate five hundred dollar contracts on the same day for the same homeowner. That is one undertaking wearing four hats, and the exemption does not apply.

The second is what six hundred dollars is not. It is not a written contract trigger. It is purely a licensure exemption threshold. When you get to the contracts chapter you will meet a different dollar figure for when an agreement must be in writing. Do not let the exam swap them on you.
Question. Six hundred dollars. What does it decide, and what does it not decide.

It decides whether you need a license for that undertaking, measured on the aggregate price, and it cannot be dodged by splitting the job. It does not decide whether your contract has to be in writing.
Idea five. How you get the license in the first place.

Four requirements. Good moral character, and for a company that reaches every partner, officer, director, member, and shareholder. Proof of identity, meaning a copy of your driver license or state I D, which the department may use only to prove identity. The sixty hour prelicensure education. And the exam.

Now notice what is not on that list. Experience. The statute has no experience requirement. A twenty two year old who has never framed a wall can hold the same license you do. People assume a trade license must require years in the field, and here it does not. Expect a question built on that assumption.

The sixty hour course has been required since June first, two thousand eight, and it has to include at least six hours in each of seven competency areas. Business management, estimating, and job costing. Design and building science. Contracts, liability, and risk management. Marketing and sales. Project management and scheduling. The current Michigan Residential Code. And MIOSHA construction safety standards.

Seven areas, six hours minimum in each, sixty hours total. Seven times six is forty two, so the remaining eighteen hours float wherever the provider wants them. And a detail worth money, the certificate never expires, as long as the course was taken after June first, two thousand eight.
One clock to remember. Once LARA receives your application, you have one year to finish everything, including passing the exam. Miss the year and your fees are forfeited and the application is void.
Question. Name the four requirements, and tell me the one thing people expect to be on the list that is not.
Good moral character, proof of identity, sixty hours of prelicensure education, and the exam. Experience is not required.
Idea six. Keeping the license once you have it.

The license runs three years. You must maintain a place of business in Michigan, and every additional location needs its own branch office license. If you are a nonresident you file a consent to service of process, which simply means Michigan can serve you with legal papers here. And your contracts must carry your license information, both your individual license and any license you hold as a qualifying officer of a company.

At renewal you state two things to the department. That you have a current copy of the Michigan Residential Code. And that you meet your continuing competency requirements. Keep your continuing education documentation for at least five years.

The hours depend on when you were first licensed, and the split year is two thousand nine. Licensed on or after January first, two thousand nine, you owe twenty one hours per three year cycle, and during your first six years at least three of those hours have to land in every calendar year, with at least three hours covering codes, safety, and changes in the law. Licensed before two thousand nine with a clean record, you owe just three hours per cycle, one hour of codes, one hour of safety, one hour of legal issues. And if you get disciplined, the department can order anywhere from three to twenty one hours in your next cycle.

If the license lapses there is a ladder, and the rung is three years. Expired less than three years, you file an application and pay one hundred eighty five dollars and you are back. Lapsed more than three years, you start over. Sixty hours of prelicensure again, application, fees, good moral character, and you retake the exam.
Question. Your license expired four years ago. What do you have to do.
Start from the beginning. Past three years there is no shortcut back. Sixty hours again, and the exam again.
Idea seven. Companies and the qualifying officer.

When a corporation, a partnership, or an L L C does the building, the law treats it as a new legal person, and that person needs its own license. The company designates a qualifying officer out of its officers, partners, members, or managing agent. That person passes the exam and must also obtain and maintain their own individual license.

What is the qualifying officer for. Supervising and controlling the construction operations so the company complies with the law. That is the whole idea. The state wants one identifiable human being answerable for how the company builds. Everyone with control in the entity has to be at least eighteen.

Now the part that makes excellent exam questions, the suspension chains. If the qualifying officer's license is suspended, revoked, or denied, the company's license is suspended. If the qualifying officer leaves the company, the company license is suspended, although the department can allow a reasonable time to qualify a replacement. And a licensee on inactive status cannot serve as a qualifying officer.
The pattern is simple once you see it. The company's license hangs on the qualifying officer. Cut that person loose and the company drops.
Question. Your qualifying officer quits on a Friday. What happens to the company license.
It is suspended. The department can give you a reasonable time to qualify a replacement, but the company does not simply carry on unaffected.
Idea eight. Discipline, and the workmanship complaint.

A homeowner has eighteen months to file a complaint. Eighteen months from the latest of completion, occupancy, or purchase on a maintenance and alteration job, or from the certificate of occupancy or the closing on a project that needs an occupancy permit.

The list of conduct that gets you disciplined is long, so learn the greatest hits. Abandonment of a project without legal excuse. Diversion of funds, which means taking money for one project and spending it on another. Failure to account for money belonging to others. Willful departure from the plans and specifications without consent. Willful violation of building laws. Failing to notify the department within ten days of a change in the control of the business. Failing to deliver the entire agreement to the purchaser. Aiding and abetting an unlicensed person, or lending out your license. Becoming insolvent or filing bankruptcy.

And one people never expect. Workmanship that does not meet the Michigan Residential Code is a discipline ground all by itself. No fraud, no theft, no complaint about your character. Bad work is enough.

Workmanship complaints have their own procedure, and the exam likes its deadlines. The homeowner sends the department a written complaint and sends you a copy at the same time. You are presumed innocent until the hearing examiner finds otherwise. Once a building inspection report verifies the complaint, the department must mail you the verified complaint by certified mail within thirty days. Miss that thirty days and the department loses the ability to fine you, though it can still pursue restitution or suspension.

And here is a tool you can actually use in your business. You may put an alternative dispute resolution clause in your contracts. If a complainant skips your contractual A D R procedure and sues you anyway, that failure is an affirmative defense.
Question. Two numbers from this segment. How long does the homeowner have to complain, and how long does the department have to mail you a verified complaint.
Eighteen months for the homeowner. Thirty days for the department, by certified mail, once the inspection report verifies it.
Last idea. Penalties, in three buckets.

Bucket one is administrative, and this is what LARA can do to you directly. Limit, suspend, deny, or revoke your license. Censure. Probation. Restitution. And an administrative fine of up to ten thousand dollars.

Bucket two is criminal, and it is for unlicensed residential building. The fines run five thousand to twenty five thousand dollars. First offense is a misdemeanor with up to one year. Second offense, up to two years. And if the unlicensed work causes death or serious injury, it becomes a felony with up to four years.

Bucket three is civil. The attorney general or a prosecutor can sue, and the court shall assess a civil fine of five thousand to twenty five thousand dollars on top of any damages. Note the word shall. That fine is not optional.
Ten thousand for the agency. Five to twenty five thousand on the criminal and civil side. If you keep those two ranges straight you will get the penalty question.

Now the consequence that matters most in real life. An unlicensed builder cannot sue to collect payment. That is section two four one two. To bring the suit you must allege and prove you were licensed during the performance of the work. No license, no lawsuit. And no construction lien either. You can do the work, do it well, and have no legal way to get paid.

One trap to bury forever. There is no such statute as M C L three thirty nine point six one one. If you see it on an answer sheet, it is invented. The penalty sections are six zero one, six zero two, and two four one two.
Question. You did twenty thousand dollars of work, you were unlicensed, the homeowner refuses to pay. What are your options in court.
You have none. No suit for payment, no lien. And you are exposed to the criminal and civil fines on top of eating the loss.
Now let us finish with exam logistics, because knowing the mechanics removes a surprising amount of test day anxiety.

PSI administers it. One hundred sixty questions. Fifty business and law, one hundred ten trade. You need one hundred sixteen correct, which is seventy two and a half percent. You get two hundred forty minutes and it is closed book.

Since November fourteenth, twenty nineteen it is one combined exam with one score. There are no separate section passes, so if you fail you retake the whole thing. Up to ten unscored experimental questions may be mixed in, which means a question that feels impossible may not even count.
The trade questions reference the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code, confirmed current in the PSI handbook updated August of twenty twenty six.

Fees. One hundred ninety five dollars to apply to LARA. One hundred seventeen dollars for the exam, and the same for a retest. The salesperson exam is a different animal, forty five questions, thirty two to pass, ninety minutes, eighty five dollars, and no education requirement.

The practical rules. No walk ins. Cancel at least two days ahead or lose your fee. Arrive thirty minutes early, because if you show up after the start time you forfeit. Bring one valid signature bearing photo I D that matches the name you registered under. Your calculator must be silent, battery powered, non printing, and have no alphabet keys, and the measurement converting construction calculators are banned. Bring a plain one.
And how you find out. If you pass, you only see the word pass. If you fail, you get section scores. There is no post exam review, so you never see which questions you missed.
Time for the rapid fire recap. I am going to say these fast. You are not learning them now, you are checking which ones you already have.

Article twenty four, Public Act two ninety nine of nineteen eighty. Nine board members, four builders, two M and A, three public. Residential structure, detached one or two family, or a townhouse of three stories or less with separate egress. Six hundred dollars, licensure exemption, aggregate price, anti splitting rule. Sixty hours prelicensure, seven areas, six hours each, effective June first two thousand eight, certificate never expires. One year to finish licensure after applying. License term, three years. Continuing competency, twenty one hours per cycle if licensed after two thousand nine, three hours per year in the first six years, and three hours per cycle if licensed before. Keep records five years. Twelve M and A crafts. Entity principals at least eighteen. Complaint window, eighteen months. Change of control notice, ten days. Verified complaint certified mail, thirty days. Administrative fine, ten thousand maximum. Criminal and civil fines, five to twenty five thousand. Jail, one year first offense, two years second, four years felony if death or serious injury. No license means no lawsuit and no lien. Exam, one sixty questions, fifty business and law, one ten trade, one sixteen to pass, two hundred forty minutes, closed book, combined since November twenty nineteen. Regulatory and statutory requirements, thirteen questions. Insurance, bonds and liens, eleven. Fees, one ninety five application, one seventeen exam, one eighty five relicensure, eighty five salesperson. And the code on the exam is the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code.

That is the chapter. Thirteen questions sitting right there. If any of the questions I asked you gave you trouble, that is your signal for where to drill, and the drill track for this chapter is the right place to do it. Go get those points.
